alalal-e85021-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 1: whether what is believed can have the testimony of reason.

alalal-e85021-d1e113.summary: Raises the doubt on the first part: whether what is believed can have the testimony of reason.

alalal-e85021-d1e122.summary: First argument: 1 Peter 3:15 tells us always to be ready to give a reason for the faith and hope in us.

alalal-e85021-d1e139.summary: Second argument: 2 Peter 1:16-17 says the apostles did not follow fables but were eyewitnesses of the glory, so contemplation of that glory was their reason for believing.

alalal-e85021-d1e152.summary: Third argument: 1 John 1:1 announces what was seen, heard and touched of the Word of life, so the senses prove faith.

alalal-e85021-d1e165.summary: Fourth argument: Paul tells Agrippa he was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, so vision was his reason for faith.

alalal-e85021-d1e176.summary: Fifth argument: Damascene says the apostles, enlightened by the Spirit and working signs, drew unbelievers from ignorance to divine knowledge with the net of miracles.

alalal-e85021-d1e197.summary: Sixth argument: Hebrews 2:3-4 says salvation was confirmed to us by those who heard, God bearing witness with signs and wonders.

alalal-e85021-d1e215.summary: Seventh argument: Chrysostom says Nathanael, doubting that anything good could come from Nazareth, showed his diligence about Scripture; so Scripture's testimony must be examined before believing an article.

alalal-e85021-d1e247.summary: Eighth argument: faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:17), and Gregory says God gives understanding by enlightening the mind about what is heard; so hearing and illumination must precede belief.

alalal-e85021-d1e271.summary: Ninth argument: Peter of Ravenna says it is not safe to believe without reason.

alalal-e85021-d1e286.summary: Tenth argument: Augustine to Paulinus: we believe things absent, but it seems fitting that testimony be given for them.

alalal-e85021-d1e300.summary: Eleventh argument, from the same: in things seen we are witnesses, in things believed we are aided by others' testimony; so faith receives reason.

alalal-e85021-d1e316.summary: Sed contra: Chrysostom on John 3:12 says one who refuses what can be grasped by thought is accused of folly, but one who refuses what cannot be grasped by thought, only by faith, is accused of unbelief; so faith is not by reasoning.

alalal-e85021-d1e350.summary: Second sed contra from the same homily: faith is needed everywhere; that the cross is the fount of life, reasoning could not easily accept, as mocking gentiles show, but faith, surpassing reason's weakness, easily accepts and holds it.

alalal-e85021-d1e374.summary: Solution: as before, faith has no merit where human reason gives proof. But Damascene's distinction applies: one faith is from hearing, another is a charism of the Holy Spirit. Faith from hearing can have an inducing, not proving, reason, not to make one consent but to make consent easier for one already inclined by affect; the charism is an infused light tending to first truth, without an inducing reason.
claims: Reasons can induce and ease the assent of faith from hearing, but never prove it.
Faith as charism is an infused light that needs no inducing reason.

alalal-e85021-d1e411.summary: Recalls Augustine's definition of believing as thinking with assent: on the side of thinking, faith admits reason, since it comes from hearing, but a reason that plays upon what is believed for delight, not for consent; on the side of consent it rests only on infused light.
claims: Reason serves the 'thinking' in faith for delight, while assent rests only on infused light.

alalal-e85021-d1e437.summary: Gives another distinction from Peter in the Itinerarium Clementis: faith requires proof only that the prophet who handed it down is true; if he is, all he teaches is true, even what is not understood because of its height.
claims: Proof is needed only for the credibility of the revealer, not for each article.

alalal-e85021-d1e457.summary: Reply to the first argument: Peter speaks of reason defending and inducing faith in a believer, not of reason producing faith.

alalal-e85021-d1e468.summary: This answers all the arguments except the last three authorities.

alalal-e85021-d1e475.summary: Reply to Peter of Ravenna: he is speaking not of faith but of a judge's belief in legal cases.

alalal-e85021-d1e485.summary: Reply to the two Augustine texts: 'believe' there is not used as in faith but for consent to something improbable that many attest.

alalal-e85021.summary: Article 1 of Distinction 24 asks whether what is believed can have the testimony of reason. Many authorities appeal to giving reasons for faith, eyewitness testimony, visions, miracles, scriptural evidence and hearing. Chrysostom insists that faith accepts what reasoning cannot. Albert holds that faith has no merit where reason gives proof, and draws Damascene's distinction. Faith from hearing can have reasons that induce and ease assent in one already inclined by affect, but never prove. Faith as a charism of the Spirit is an infused light needing no such reason. On Augustine's definition, reason serves the thinking in faith for delight, while assent rests on infused light. Peter's distinction in the Clementine Recognitions adds that proof is needed only that the revealing prophet is truthful. 1 Peter 3:15 concerns reasons that defend faith, and the other authorities use 'believe' for judicial or human belief.
claims: Faith has no merit where reason provides proof.
Reasons can induce and ease the assent of faith but do not cause or prove it; assent rests on infused light.
Proof is needed only for the credibility of the revealer, not for each article.
